text:
LIFE LESSONS FROM HIGHWAY

Work with a realistic aim daily if you will push hard one day next two days will be disturbed (80 kmph but constant)

Don't take long breaks, drive steady at 80 but remember the race is long

Don't look back or don't compare yourself with others. If you will keep looking back to check how much is the distance you will never be able to increase it

While driving where you will look in sides you will learn towards that side automatically means stay in your lane and follow your path

When there is fog in the way and path is not clear, it's better to slow down and let others overtake

Follow the ahead car carefully and maintain distance so that you don't repeat his mistake or affected by his mistake.

Something weather is clear and road is empty then follow the fast car. Means a good and consistent competitor can take you much ahead in your journey.

Before going out for the journey it is must to know your destination.

Timing is also important, if you will start your journey early morning then you will get less traffic but in winters you will get more fog

One break in the way can break your vehicle not 1 lakh km of straight road.

Don't drink and drive, don't do a mistake which can impact your whole life. Like scrolling whole day

The way car should be clean always, similarly dress and adress gives your first impression

A good car is a car which makes your journey done smoothly and which is in your budget WHICH CAN GET THINGS DONE, you should get things done

Sometimes google maps shows you wrong way but using common sense is important don't follow everything blindly.

If you are running a car since years then you will be a master of it. Similarly if you give enough practice and time to one thing. it will becomes your second nature

If a path is too straight and simple without hurdle then there is no fun and you won't enjoy the process

आज नेपाल एउटा निकै कठिन र कारुणिक मोडबाट गुज्रिरहेको छ। हालै आएको विनाशकारी बाढी र पहिरोले (Fluids/Floods) नेपाललाई वर्षौं पछाडि धकेलिदिएको छ। यो विपत्तिले केवल भौतिक संरचना मात्र भत्काएको छैन, बरु नेपालीहरूलाई आफ्ना प्रियजन, आफ्नो थातथलो र पुस्तौंदेखिको सभ्यताबाट समेत अलग गराइदिएको छ।

आज नेपालका गाउँ-बस्तीहरूको अवस्था हेर्दा आँखा रसाउँछन्। कयौँ आमाहरूको काख रित्तिएको छ, कतिपय छोराछोरीले आफ्ना आमाबुबा गुमाएका छन्। कति त पूरै परिवार नै एकाएक विलीन भएका छन्। बाढीले बगाएर ल्याएको हिलो र दलदलको बीचमा आज केवल भत्किएका घरका भग्नावशेष र भग्नावशेष मात्र देखिन्छन्। नेपालको सम्पूर्ण प्रणाली, पूर्वाधार र जनजीवन पूर्ण रूपमा अस्तव्यस्त भएको छ। मानिसहरू खुल्ला आकाशमुनि आधारभूत आवश्यकताका लागि छटपटाइरहेका छन्।

सर, हजुरको एउटा आवाजमा ठूलो शक्ति छ। आज भारतमा मात्र होइन, नेपालमा पनि हजुरलाई औधी मन पराउने, सम्मान गर्ने र हजुरका कुरा सुन्ने लाखौँ प्रसंशक र विद्यार्थीहरू छन्। नेपाली समाजले हजुरलाई आफ्नै अभिभावक सरह मान्छ। यो अत्यन्तै संवेदनशील र गम्भीर परिस्थितिमा हजुरले नेपालको तर्फबाट केही बोलिदिनुहुन र आफ्नो तर्फबाट तथा आफ्ना प्रसंशकहरूलाई समेटी नेपालका लागि केही राहत वा मद्दतको पहल गरिदिनुहुन हार्दिक अनुरोध गर्दछौँ।

हजुरको सानो प्रयास वा एउटा सन्देशले पनि अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय स्तरमा ध्यानाकर्षण गराउन र नेपालका पीडितहरूका लागि ठूलो सहायता जुटाउन मद्दत पुग्नेछ। नेपाल आज निकै गहिरो संकटमा छ र हजुर जस्तो मानवीय मन भएको व्यक्तित्वको साथको पर्खाइमा छ। कृपया नेपाललाई यो दलदलबाट उठ्न मद्दत गर्नुहोस्।

आदरणीय खान सर,

पिछले कुछ दिनों से आपके बारे में तरह-तरह की बातें और आरोप सुनने को मिल रहे हैं। ऐसे समय में आपके लाखों छात्र और शुभचिंतक आपके साथ खड़े हैं। जो व्यक्ति वर्षों से शिक्षा के माध्यम से युवाओं को आगे बढ़ाने का काम करता आया हो, उसके योगदान को कुछ दिनों की विवादित चर्चाओं से नहीं आँका जा सकता।

कठिन परिस्थितियाँ इंसान की परीक्षा लेती हैं, लेकिन वही परिस्थितियाँ उसकी मजबूती भी साबित करती हैं। हमें विश्वास है कि आप धैर्य, संयम और सच्चाई के साथ इस दौर का सामना करेंगे।

आपने लाखों विद्यार्थियों को संघर्ष करना और हार न मानना सिखाया है। आज वही विद्यार्थी आपके लिए प्रार्थना कर रहे हैं कि आप पहले की तरह मजबूती से आगे बढ़ें।

ईश्वर आपको शक्ति, साहस और स्वस्थ जीवन प्रदान करें।

हम आपके साथ हैं सर। 🙏

खान सर।
सबसे पहले आपको प्रणाम।
आपका हॉस्पिटल खोलने का वीडियो देखा , बहुत ही सराहनीय कार्य है जिससे ग़रीबों, असहाय,और वंचितों को सहायता मिलेगी।
मगर सर समाज में कुछ ऐसे लोग भी हैं जिन्होंने इसे धंधा बनाया हुआ है,उन लोगों को आपका कार्य पसंद तो नहीं आयेगा, लेकिन हमें उनसे कोई मतलब नहीं,जो जैसा करेगा उसका कर्म उसका पीछा करेगा।
लेकिन सर आपसे एक विनम्र निवेदन है ,कि हमे चोट पहुंचाने,या हमे नीचे गिराने वाले हमारे आस पास के लोग ही होते है,जिस पर हम ज्यादा भरोसा जताते है।
सर आपसे विनेदन है कि आप हमेशा सचेत रहें और हमारी दुआ है कि आप हमेशा स्वस्थ रहे।
सर हमने समाज से आप जैसे सोचने वाले और कार्य करने वाले सर राजीव दीक्षित को हमने खो दिया , इसलिए मुझे डर लगता है।
इसलिए आपसे विनेदन है कि आप जीवन में हमेशा स्वस्थ रहें और सचेत रहें।
हम सब की दुवाएं सदैव आपके साथ है।

जय हिंद! ख़ान सर, कृपया अपना सुझाव दें। हमारे देश में आये दिन अपराध और आतंकी घटनाएँ होती रहती हैं। कई बार दोषी — जैसे अपराधी, बलात्कारी और आतंकवादी — जमानत पर, झूठे बयानों के आधार पर, या राजनीतिक समर्थन के चलते खुलेआम घूमते रहते हैं। कुछ आतंकवादियों को तो समझौतों के तहत वापस भेज भी दिया जाता है। वहीं मुकदमे वर्षों तक चलते रहते हैं।
दूसरी ओर, हमारे देश में बहुत से लोग — मासूम बच्चे, युवा, नवविवाहित और अन्य — किडनी और लीवर फेल होने जैसी गंभीर स्वास्थ्य समस्याओं से जूझ रहे हैं। ऐसे में क्यों न ऐसा नियम बनाया जाए कि जिन्हें अदालत ने दोषी ठहराया हो, विशेष रूप से गंभीर अपराधों में, उनके अंगों (किडनी, लीवर आदि) को ज़रूरतमंदों के लिए सरकार द्वारा दान करवा दिया जाए, चाहे कुछ शुल्क लेकर या नि:शुल्क — और इसके बाद कानूनी प्रक्रिया जारी रहे।
इससे अच्छे लोगों की जान बच सकती है और अपराधियों के मन में डर भी पैदा होगा। कृपया इस विचार पर मार्गदर्शन दें।

Dear Sir ne is video '90-Day Maths Winter Arc' par focus karta hai. Ye strategy class 10th ke students ke liye hai taaki wo boards mein 90+ score kar sakein.

Main Points and Strategy:

1. Winter Arc ka Concept (0:30-1:38):
October se December tak ka samay ek 'training phase' hai.
Jis tarah anime characters akele training karte hain, waise hi students ko in 3 mahino mein discipline maintain karna chahiye.

2. Rules for Success (3:52-13:21):
Rule 1: Sahi samay par utho (3:59-5:10): Fix time banao, chahe wo koi bhi ho, lekin usse change mat karo. Zaroori nahi ki sirf 4 baje utho, bas consistency rakho.
Rule 2: Daily Maths practice (5:13-5:58): Maths dekhne se nahi, karne se aati hai. Rozana 1-1.5 ghante practice zaroori hai.
Rule 3: Phone se duri (5:59-8:10): Padhai ke waqt phone ko apne se dur rakho. Phone ka addiction aapka time waste karta hai, jo 90 days mein 45 hours ka loss de sakta hai.
Rule 4: Monthly Planning (8:12-10:52):
October: Syllabus complete karo aur saare concepts clear karo.
November: Full book ka revision karo, saare formulas aur notes revise karo.
December: Sample papers aur Previous Year Questions (PYQs) solve karo.
Rule 5: Daily tracking (10:54-11:23): Raat ko 2 minute mein check karo ki aaj kya padha aur kitna target pura hua.

I watched the full video and make notes also

3. Mindset aur Discipline (11:34-13:21):
Jab padhne ka mann na ho, tabhi asli discipline test hoti hai.
'Don't miss anything twice': Agar ek din miss ho gaya to chalo theek hai, lekin usse lagatar do din mat hone do.

The book contains only 8 chapters, out of which Chapters 7 and 8 are largely based on Class 10 Mathematics. Some topics from other chapters also belong to the Class 10 syllabus. This video is a comprehensive one-shot revision session for Class 11 English, covering grammar, literature, and writing skills to help students prepare for their exams.

Grammar Revision (1:13 - 28:28)

The session provides a deep dive into English Tenses and Clause types:

Tenses: The instructor explains the importance of identifying cues in sentences (like "yesterday" or "since morning") to correctly choose between tenses, with a special focus on the common combination of Past Indefinite and Past Perfect (1:44 - 5:10).
Clauses: The instructor defines and differentiates between Noun clauses, Adjective clauses, and Adverb clauses, offering practice exercises to help students identify them correctly in exam settings (20:07 - 23:30).

Writing Section Strategy (29:19 - 41:00)

Guidance is provided on how to approach the 16-mark writing section:

Advertisements: Tips for writing clear, concise notices for "For Sale" or "Situation Vacant" (30:27 - 33:15).
Poster Writing: Emphasizes the use of capital letters, catchy slogans, and simple drawings to grab attention (34:01 - 35:22).
Speech & Debate: Structural advice on how to address an audience (e.g., "Good morning, respected Principal...") and how to effectively present views for or against a motion (35:23 - 38:05).
Report Writing: Briefly covers the distinction between magazine and newspaper reports (40:07 - 40:55).

The session concludes with words of encouragement, reminding students that despite technical difficulties, the focus remains on consistent practice and preparation.

Sasha Mirchandani suggests keeping pitch decks simple, clear, and under 10 slides. He prioritizes clarity of thought over cluttered, data-heavy presentations.

Recommended structure:

1. Team: Introduce the founding team first.
2. Problem: Clearly define the specific pain point.
3. Solution: Provide a concise answer to the problem.
4. Why Now: Explain the timing and why the market is ready for this solution at this exact moment.
5. Product/Demo: Show a simple visual demonstration or video of the product.
6. Traction: Highlight key metrics or progress to show early validation.
7. Competition: Provide a clear, honest view of the market landscape.
8. Ask: State exactly how much capital you are looking to raise.

If this doesn’t fit the main podcast format, perhaps a separate YouTube channel or series like “Kids by Raj Shamani” could be created — where kids from different backgrounds, young innovators, curious students, and even ordinary kids can share their stories and ideas.

I genuinely believe the purpose should be more than just entertainment — it could be about giving young minds a voice, confidence, and exposure. 🙌

From NYPD to Secret Service: (03:25) Evy describes her transition from the NYPD to the Secret Service and the rigorous multi-step selection process.
The Selection Process: (09:17) Details on the brutal nature of the agency's hiring process, including extensive background checks, polygraphs, and panel interviews.
Operational Training: (13:22) Insights into the specialized training agents undergo, including combat, tactical driving with ballistic vehicles, and ethical decision-making.

text:
📱 Phone away while working
Not beside you, even on silent. Put it in another room/ out of eyesight /covered in a box may be.
One task at a time
Multitasking = attention switching.
45 min focus → 10 min break
Repeat 2–3 times instead of forcing hours of continuous work.
Learn → Close → Recall → Apply
After studying, close the material and write 3–5 things you remember. Then use them.
Control short-form content
Don't randomly open Reels/Shorts throughout the day. Keep a fixed time window.
Find your peak brain hours
Notice when you're naturally most focused and reserve that time for difficult work.
Don't chase the 5 AM lifestyle
The goal is good sleep + your best cognitive hours, not waking up at a particular time.
Let your brain be bored sometimes
Walk, shower, drink tea without constantly consuming content.
The one formula to remember:

Less stimulation → deeper focus → better memory → better learning.

And for your studying/career work:

Phone away → 45 min deep work → 10 min break → recall what you learned → apply it.

text:
Top 10 Takeaways:
1. The Cost of Task-Switching: Every time you switch your attention, your brain pays a biological "switching tax," which significantly lowers your productivity (1:17 - 1:30).
2. Digital Hygiene: Your phone reduces cognitive capacity even when switched off and face-down on your desk. Keep it out of reach to truly focus (50:32 - 59:18).
3. Rewire Your Identity: You can change your beliefs and behavior by creating a "new story" for yourself. The Default Mode Network (DMN) in your brain helps integrate these new stories into your identity (16:25 - 17:30).
4. Implementation Intentions: Use "If-Then" plans to automate habits. Be as specific as possible (e.g., "When my alarm goes off at 11 PM, I will immediately brush my teeth") to avoid relying on willpower (27:08 - 31:00).
5. Emotional Regulation: Most bad habits (like doom-scrolling) are attempts to cope with negative emotions. To break a habit, you must first identify the underlying feeling (stress, overwhelm) and then insert a "cognitive pause" (43:23 - 47:30).
6. The Myth of Multitasking: Your brain is physically incapable of multitasking; it is actually just rapidly switching between tasks, which causes mental fatigue and lowers performance (1:03:53).
7. The Power of Boredom: To get incredible ideas, you must cultivate space. Simply being bored and doing nothing allows the brain to make unique connections (1:48 - 1:56).
8. Content Diet: Short-form content provides "novelty" that acts like candy for the brain-tasting good in the moment but providing no memory or learning. Favor long-form content (like podcasts or documentaries) for better empathy, memory, and connection (1:28:42 - 1:37:21).
9. Chronotypes: Don't follow the "5 AM Club" trend blindly. Everyone has a different biological clock; finding your peak performance hours is more important than waking up at an arbitrary early time (2:03:33 - 2:11:32).
10. The 3M Framework for Rest: Use the 3M framework for breaks-Micro (10 mins/day), Meso (2 hours/week), and Macro (half day/ month) to prevent burnout (2:34:36 - 2:34:47).

I don’t know how many people from different countries will see this, but I hope this message reaches those who still believe that climate change is someone else’s problem.
Nepal is facing the devastating consequences of a disaster that has taken lives, destroyed homes and infrastructure, displaced communities, and shattered livelihoods. For many families, this is not a statistic—it is everything they had.
And yet, Nepal contributes only around 0.05% of global annual CO₂ emissions, according to the latest available 2024 data. In comparison, China accounts for about 31.8%, the United States 12.7%, and India 8.3% of global annual CO₂ emissions.
This is not about blaming ordinary people in any country. It is about responsibility, fairness, and climate justice.
Countries that have contributed far more to global emissions have a greater responsibility to help vulnerable nations adapt to a changing climate and recover from climate-related loss and damage.
Nepal did not create this crisis, but Nepal is paying a heavy price for it.
We are not asking for sympathy alone.
We are asking for action, accountability, climate finance, stronger disaster preparedness, and meaningful support for communities that are suffering losses they did little to cause.
The climate crisis does not respect borders. Neither should our responsibility to protect the people who are most vulnerable to it.
Nepal may contribute little to global emissions, but our people should not have to pay the greatest price.
The world must listen.
The world must act.
And climate justice must mean something.

Yes, this is AI-made — because nowadays, people seem to listen more to AI than to a real human voice, real facts, and real emotions.

Vaibhav Sisinty is good at talking about AI tools and getting people excited about them, but in his episodes, the conversation lean heavily towards the “AI changes everything / use these 20 tools” side of things.

text:
What I understand about AI is that it’s much more than just a chatbot or a tool for generating content. AI can be used in complex workflows like research, automation, routine tasks, data management, and even communication.

For example, AI could automatically organize and filter emails, draft or send WhatsApp messages, manage repetitive tasks, help with business workflows, and connect different tools together.

I also think one of the biggest advantages of AI is learning. You can use it to understand almost any topic in a clean, structured, and precise way — breaking complex concepts into something easier to understand.

Basically, I see AI as a kind of intelligent assistant that can help with research, learning, communication, automation, and everyday work, rather than just a tool for asking questions.😊

text:
Vaibhav and Raj, my main feedback is that several questions and demonstrations begin, but the conversation moves to another tool or topic before we see the complete answer or result. Some explanations remain conceptual, which makes it difficult to actually build what you’re describing.

For example, around 45:51, Vaibhav says he’ll use Hermes to build the research system, but the discussion shifts to Grok Bot. You return to Hermes later, but demonstrate analytics instead of completing that research workflow.

These are the questions I was still left with:

1. 44:14 onwards: How do we actually build the complete research/topic-discovery system in Hermes?

2. 1:03:15–1:04:18: Did the Metricool integration succeed? What analytics and automated report did the new Hermes agent produce?

3. 1:05:07: You mentioned showing the output of your own advanced system towards the end. Could we see that walkthrough?

4. 1:09:48 onwards: What was Codex’s final answer to the live question about declining ROI and the metrics to optimize?

5. 40:22; 1:38:39 onwards: How does the posting stage work? It was introduced as part of the content system but never demonstrated.

6. 17:14–18:36: How do we set up the automation that reads YouTube watch history, filters relevant videos, extracts transcripts and creates JSON cards?

7. 18:40–20:27: How do Slack conversations and meeting transcripts automatically enter the second brain?

8. 20:29–21:23: How are conversations from different AI tools exported daily and brought into one memory system?

9. 21:17–29:40: How do we actually install and connect the Cognee memory layer to the agents?

10. 52:43; 1:19:21 onwards: How do we launch the agent swarm, share the required context and combine its results?

11. 1:17:48–1:23:20: What is the actual scoring rubric for ranking topics and angles? Could you show one worked example using the DNA playbook?

12. 1:24:55–1:25:43: How do you test the ten packaging options through ads and choose the winning title/thumbnail?

13. 1:28:47–1:30:34: What exact script structure does the agent follow? Could we see the skill and a complete example, including the hook, body and ending?

14. 1:35:55–1:38:12: How is the corrected evaluation system built so an agent cannot give itself fake scores? Could you show the separate generator and evaluator setup?

I understand some tasks take time. But when an agent is left working in the background, please return to its output before ending the episode. And when a question leads into another topic, please come back and finish the original thread.

A follow-up episode completing these workflows, with the setup, instructions and final outputs visible, would make the discussion much easier to put into practice.

Experiment this and see how this goes and if it goes well then hire an expert to maximize that capability, you see here you are using AI as a lever to maximize and outcome and putting human in the loop after the fact. I’ve seen this work better in tech too. I would focus on levers outside your teams capability to improve your outcomes (reach) where even an average performance will lead to better upside.

Summary / Quick Notes for everyone saving time:

🧠 Daily Habits to Optimize Your Brain & Focus:
☀ Morning Sunlight: Get 10–15 minutes of outdoor light within an hour of waking to set your circadian clock and boost daytime alertness.
⏳ Delay Caffeine (90–120 mins): Let your natural adenosine clear out first to prevent afternoon energy crashes.
🎯 90-Minute Focus Blocks: Work in focused ultradian cycles without multitasking; take 10 minutes of mental downtime afterward.
⚡ Dopamine Control: Attach dopamine to the effort and process, not just the reward, to stay consistently driven without burning out.
🫁 Physiological Sigh for Stress: Two quick inhales through the nose followed by a long, slow exhale through the mouth to rapidly lower heart rate.
🌙 Sleep Hygiene: Keep the room dark and cool, and avoid bright overhead screens/lights 1–2 hours before bed.

Like/pin this if you found it useful! 📌

text:
Key Points
🧠 Synchronize Hormones for Peak Performance: High morning cortisol via bright light and hydration activates daytime energy, while low nighttime cortisol plus dim light enhances melatonin for restorative sleep and immunity. (00:10-00:24, 00:53-00:59)
🌙 Turn Off the Mind to Sleep Better: Practices like yoga nidra, deliberate breathing with extended exhales, and an eye-movement routine disrupt proprioception and quiet mental chatter, enabling falling and returning to sleep. (00:24-00:34)
💪 Build Mental Resilience Incrementally: Controlled physical and psychological stress, e.g., cold exposure or pushing workout intensity, strengthens nervous system adaptability and courage over time. (01:05-01:14, 01:43-01:47)
🔄 Balance Drive with Rest: Intense early career effort (years 1–3) should transition to regulating stress and recovery later, fostering sustainable peak performance and leadership capacity. (00:51-01:05)
🎯 Focus on Controllable Factors: Using tools like the “left vs. right column” exercise helps distinguish anxieties outside control versus actionable steps, improving mental clarity and stress management. (00:26-00:28)
🤝 Surround with Supportive Community: Strong friendships, a trustworthy social circle, and mentors provide accountability and grounding to navigate pressures and stress. (00:50-00:56)
🎭 Handle Public Criticism with Perspective: Maintain mental immunity by remembering critics’ struggles stem from their own pain, preserving self-belief and compassion. (00:56-01:04)
🧩 Understand the Neuroscience of Choking and Risk: Overthinking potential gain or loss can paralyze performance; lowering stakes and focusing on “one step at a time” practices prevent freezing under pressure. (01:14-01:27)
🔥 New Concept – Clutch States: Beyond flow, clutch states define sustained effort near one’s limits essential for mastery and high-level performance. (01:36-01:41)
🧘 Learning is a Process of Error and Rewiring: Mistakes trigger neuroplasticity; self-testing and iterative learning reinforce skills and confidence. (01:41-01:43)
🧒 Mentality Shift from Victim to Agent: Winners transmute challenges into generative action through deliberate mindset work, gradual self-regulation, and seeking support as needed. (01:33-01:41)
🕹️ Be a Creator, Not Just a Consumer: Actively producing content, ideas, or solutions engages the brain deeply and fosters long-term fulfillment over passive consumption. (01:28-01:30)
❤️ Love Requires Patience and Building Trust: Deep, lasting romantic connection stems from friendship, mutual trust, and slowing down the typical fast-paced relationship trajectory. (02:06-02:18)
🙏 In Crisis, Seek Help and Let Go of Total Control: At one’s lowest points, acknowledging vulnerability and asking for spiritual or external support helps stabilize before reengaging with life. (02:00-02:13)
🌟 Identity is a Verb: Who you are is shaped through repeated acts and mindset shifts, not fixed traits or titles. Incremental wins build new identities. (01:40-01:45)

text:
My notes (2/09/2026) — for myself, not for validation.
Understanding body + mind → design your environment around reality, not just willpower. (Linking information psychologically + physiologically helps it stick long-term, rather than relying on half-assed motivation)
Cortisol: higher around waking → gradually decreases → lowest at night.
Morning: consistent wake time + outdoor light + movement + hydration + focused work.
Consistent bedtime matters too.
Watching half → taking what I need → coming back → continuing.

03/09/2026 :
For overthinking, more thinking isn’t always the solution.

Brain dump everything on paper.
Separate what I can control vs. what I can’t control.
Drop the uncontrollable and turn the controllable into the next immediate action.

The part I want to apply: I don’t need to solve my whole life in my head. I need to identify what is in my control and act on that.
Also, learning something → applying what I need → returning later and continuing is better than feeling like I must finish everything in one sitting.

The biggest takeaway for me: winners and losers don’t necessarily feel different — they respond differently.
Fear, doubt, despair and frustration are part of pursuing difficult goals. The goal isn’t to eliminate those feelings, but to take the next productive action despite them.
The 3 stages also stood out:
Grind → Regulate → Master
* Grind: build competence through volume and friction.
* Regulate: learn to manage energy, stress and consistency.
* Master: develop pattern recognition and intuition through experience.

And NSDR/Yoga Nidra is recovery not laziness it’s part of performance. You can’t continuously push a depleted mind and expect high-quality work.

Feel bad → regulate → act anyway → repeat → build mastery.

⚡ Consumer to Producer:

The Dopamine Trap: Algorithms are engineered to hook you, turning consumption into a passive distraction.
The False Productivity: Consuming feels like work, but it drains your energy and focus without creating any real output.
The Identity Shift: Measure your days by what you create (code, writing, projects), not what you consume.
Actionable Rule: Protect your peak energy for production. Use consumption strictly as a targeted tool, never as a default habit.

text:
Listening to Sanjiv Goenka give long lectures about business, success and values on a podcast is interesting—but success stories should come with the full context.

There’s no denying his achievements, but he also comes from a powerful business family and inherited a significant business legacy from his father, R.P. Goenka. His group has also been involved in substantial political funding through electoral bonds and electoral trusts, while some of his companies have faced questions around coal-related matters.

So yes, talk about entrepreneurship, leadership and success. But also talk about privilege, political connections, corporate influence and the controversies along the way.

Because building a business with an inherited head start is not the same as building one from zero.

Before giving the world a lecture on success, it’s worth telling the complete story behind that success.

Yes, I am struggling. But I am also brave, disciplined, and intelligent enough to keep moving forward.

text:
With due respect sir, I feel there is an inherent contradiction in the messaging around 'Not Buying a House at a Young Age'

I completely agree that later on in life, one has so much more clarity on one's requirements with more income at one's disposal to buy a house. However, if one's income is higher in their late 30s, their expenses and responsibilities are way higher as well. So, I am not sure in %terms, is anyone better off waiting.

Secondly, it's been pointed out in the video that asset growth has significantly outstripped salary increases. As shown, one way is to invest consistently and hope to achieve a corpus to buy a house later in life.

However, another way is to buy a smaller house early on, get a foot in the door and wait for capital appreciation. Although houses are not liquid, they are not volatile as well like Stock markets which can be at their lowest at the exact moment you need to withdraw

So, this decision is much more nuanced than a simple advice to delay this decision always

Money matters, but character matters more. ❤️

text:
Hi Ankur Sir, I respect your opinion, but I’ve been living in Indore for the last 5 years, and I’d like to share my personal experience.

Indore has become quite expensive rent, petrol, healthcare, property prices, stamp duty, and daily expenses are all high, while traffic has also increased. Even cheaper flats/houses often don’t have a good living environment. I also feel there is too much corruption, politics, and favoritism in some places.

Water is another big summer problem. Borewells often stop working, and we have to pay for water tankers. Last summer, I paid ₹2,000 for a 6,000-litre tanker. Drinking water is a separate issue, and it also becomes very expensive during the summer.

Many IT companies still consider Indore a low-cost city and offer lower packages, and my company and many others are no longer offering WFH. I lived in Bangalore for 5 years and had a better experience there. I’m planning to move to Pune next year for better IT and career opportunities.

Just sharing my personal experience of the other side of living in Indore.

My question to Meta AI & it's Reply...

Yes, it's possible. Your idea is very good.

I have calculated based on today's (Sep 12, 2026) NAV - What will be the NAV if all 34 Stocks go back to their ATH / 52W High?

Calculation:

- Today's Direct NAV = ₹89.48
- If all Holdings go to ATH, NAV = ₹117.10
- That means +30.9% higher

- Today's Regular NAV = ₹81.52 -> At ATH it will be *₹106.68*.

How did I calculate?
I took the Upside from the Drawdown of each Stock.
For example: HDFC Bank has 7.63% weight, has fallen 32%. If it goes to ATH, it has to rise 47%. So its contribution to NAV is 7.63% x 47% = 3.59% Contribution.
ITC has fallen 37.6%, if it goes to ATH it has to rise 60% - that is the biggest Upside.

What does this mean:
PP Flexicap is now 31% below its Potential ATH NAV. If the Market goes up again, this Fund has the power to go up as fast as it fell. That's why they are holding 15% Cash - to buy when it falls.

6/10 Marks only. Pranjal being your committed viewer, I would like to bring out following points: You produced this video on the basis of discussion with White Oak guy, he only proposed this logic which is not correct as far as Passive active investment cycle is concerned.
At conceptual level & face value this sounds correct, however this theory fails to pass the litmus test time, and it only applies to those index funds where Basket is very small like Nifty 50, but when you expand this to beyond that basket this theory falls face front. Eg. Midcap 150 or Total Market funds etc..
Why there was no used case or a case study of a mature regulated market included in your video, probably because there are no known cases available yet since ETFs were first time introduced by Blackrock in US S&P500. More importantly ETFs and Index funds are also regulated by similar policies as active fund where investors safeguards are kept in place. This video sounds less like an educational information but more like scaremongering.
Anyways I am still your appreciator and will continue to be so for your honesty and well researched independent thinking content for masses.

Regards & Best Wishes.

You’re absolutely correct. But with health and term insurance scams and claim denials happening almost every day, even with some of the biggest insurance providers, what’s the actual point? We’re paying ₹1 lakh or more every year for health insurance, and yet companies are denying claims left and right when people actually need the coverage. With term insurance, the entire purpose is to make sure your family is financially protected if something happens to you. Insurance is supposed to provide peace of mind, not leave families fighting for the money they were promised.

text:
Interesting analysis, especially the observation that the US outperformed during each of the Indian “sideways” phases while India subsequently outperformed strongly during the up-cycles. To me, that actually makes a strong case for geographic diversification rather than choosing only India or only the US.

One small point on the final 29-year comparison: if S&P 500 CAGR is 8.08% and INR depreciation is 3.06%, the two effects should compound rather than simply be added. Using the figures in the video, that gives roughly 11.39%, rather than 11.14%. So the historical gap versus Nifty's 11.86% narrows to only around 0.47% CAGR.

There is another interesting aspect of the sideways periods. While Indian equities were producing very low returns during those specific periods, the S&P 500 was still generating positive CAGR. That means capital invested in the US continued compounding during years when an Indian investor was experiencing little capital appreciation. Over a 6-8 year sideways period, even a few percentage points of annual return can create a meaningful difference in terminal wealth because each year's return compounds on the previous year's gains. Of course, this does not prove that the US will behave the same way in future sideways periods, but I think this opportunity-cost/compounding effect is worth including in the comparison.

text:
*जय हनुमान ज्ञान गुन सागर।
जय कपीस तिहुं लोक उजागर।।

राम दूत अतुलित बल धामा।
अंजनि-पुत्र पवनसुत नामा।।

महाबीर बिक्रम बजरंगी।
कुमति निवार सुमति के संगी।।

कंचन बरन बिराज सुबेसा।
कानन कुण्डल कुँचित केसा।।

हाथ बज्र औ ध्वजा बिराजे।
कांधे मूंज जनेउ साजे।।

शंकर सुवन केसरी नंदन।
तेज प्रताप महा जग वंदन।।

बिद्यावान गुनी अति चातुर।
राम काज करिबे को आतुर।।

प्रभु चरित्र सुनिबे को रसिया।
राम लखन सीता मन बसिया।।

सूक्ष्म रूप धरि सियहिं दिखावा।
बिकट रूप धरि लंक जरावा।।

भीम रूप धरि असुर संहारे।
रामचन्द्र के काज संवारे।।

लाय सजीवन लखन जियाये।
श्री रघुबीर हरषि उर लाये।।

रघुपति कीन्ही बहुत बड़ाई।
तुम मम प्रिय भरतहि सम भाई।।

सहस बदन तुम्हरो जस गावैं।
अस कहि श्रीपति कण्ठ लगावैं।।

सनकादिक ब्रह्मादि मुनीसा।
नारद सारद सहित अहीसा।।

जम कुबेर दिगपाल जहां ते।
कबि कोबिद कहि सके कहां ते।।

तुम उपकार सुग्रीवहिं कीन्हा।
राम मिलाय राज पद दीन्हा।।

तुम्हरो मंत्र बिभीषन माना।
लंकेश्वर भए सब जग जाना।।

जुग सहस्र जोजन पर भानु।
लील्यो ताहि मधुर फल जानू।।

प्रभु मुद्रिका मेलि मुख माहीं।
जलधि लांघि गये अचरज नाहीं।।

दुर्गम काज जगत के जेते।
सुगम अनुग्रह तुम्हरे तेते।।

राम दुआरे तुम रखवारे।
होत न आज्ञा बिनु पैसारे।।

सब सुख लहै तुम्हारी सरना।
तुम रच्छक काहू को डर ना।।

आपन तेज सम्हारो आपै।
तीनों लोक हांक तें कांपै।।

भूत पिसाच निकट नहिं आवै।
महाबीर जब नाम सुनावै।।*

text:
Bhaiya meri age 26 hai aur mai physics ka teacher hu. Mai bhi apne students ko yahi samjhata hu. Iske liye maine ek example bhi diya tha jo ki probability chapter se tha.

Ex. Tha ki maan lo ek dice 🎲 hai aur mai aapke saamne ek situation rakhu ki jab dice mein 1 and 2 aayega tab aap jeetoge aur jab 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 aayega toh mai jeetunga. Toh students aapka pehla question hoga ki sir aap toh cheating kar rahe ho. Toh mera answer hoga Haan. But in apps walo ka answer hoga na. Kyonki jaise jaise dice ko uchhalne ka number badhega waise hi meri jeetne ki possibility bhi badhegi. Kyonki dice mein number hote hain 6 aur aap jeetoge do baar. Means 2/6 = 1/3 means 0.33 aur jabki mera hoga 4/6 means 2/3 = 0.666666

Yaani ki agar mai dice ko 200 baar uchhalunga toh aap 66 baar jeetoge aur mai 134 baar. Jab tak dice kam baar uchhlega tab tak aapka aur mera winning percentage same rahega. But number of figure increase hote hi mai hi jeeta raha hounga.

Tab students ko samajh mein aaya tha. 😊😊

text:
We got independence due to the aftermath of WW2, along with the contribution of our brave freedom fighters. It is a hard statement, but let me give my assessment.

WW2 made the British empire economically weaker, and they were no longer the super power of the world. The same thing happened with France.

That's why ~25 countries got freedom b/w 1945 and 1960, who were colonies of Britain and France in Asia.

Later, this independence wave hit Africa and ~45 countries got independence b/w 1960-1970.

A similar case is with Latin America's countries where most of the countries got freedom in the 19th century due to the collapse of the Spanish and Portuguese empires.

Bottom line: Freedom fighters across countries were fighting for the independence of their country, and they were indeed creating problems for the empires, but once the economic situation of these empires got weak, they were unable to hold on to their colonies and had to leave them.

However, there is one thing which I am proud of is that India got Full-independence and not the Dominion-state of the British like Canada or Australia. Credit for it should be given to our great freedom fighters only.

text:
In the Manusmriti and the Purusha Sukta of the Rigveda, society is organized as a strict hierarchy. The four groups, Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra are textually ranked according to their cosmic origin, distinct ritual purity, and legal privileges.
Under the "Twice-Born" (Dwija) framework, the upper classes held exclusive rights to Vedic study and ritual authority, while legal codes prescribed differential punishments based entirely on one's position in this social pyramid. Understanding these texts provides vital context on how structural stratification was codified in antiquity.

आप रोज कहानी सुनाते हो और आज में आपको सुनाता हूं।

ओला , उबर , रैपिडो हरियाणा के लोग बुक करके लेकर जाते है। रस्ते में टॉयलेट या फिर उल्टी का बहाना करके गाड़ी रुकवा लेते हैं। उसके बाद होता असली खेल शुरू
एक आदमी गाड़ी से बाहर उतर जाता है टॉयलेट के बहाने से
और उसको टॉयलेट भी नहीं आता है। लेकिन वह उतरता है कि कोई आ तो नहीं रहा आगे पीछे। फिर वो बहार से इशारा करता है अंदर बैठे लोगों को।

फिर अंदर बैठे लोग पीछे से ड्राइवर के गले में रस्सी डालकर फांसी लगा देते है।

उसके बाद या तो गाड़ी लेकर फरार हो जाते हैं।
या डेड बॉडी को आग लगा देते है। पता नहीं । कितने ड्राइवर ल पता हो चुके है।

जब पुलिस ने उसके घर को बताया कि आपका परिवार का सदस्य यहां पड़ा हे उसके अंदर आग लगी हुई है अभी
जब वो यहां से गये सिस्टम ने क्या बोला पता हे। आप इस डेड बॉडी को अकेले मत लेकर जाइए यहां आपके साथ कोई हादसा हो सकता है।

हमारा तो मर गया। किसी और के साथ ऐसा ना हो
यह बहुत सीरियस केस हैं। हर दिन यह होता है आप यूट्यूब पर वीडियो भी देख सकते हो।

The newly appointed CEO of the Ram Temple Trust, Air Marshal (Retd.) Jeetendra Mishra, has publicly praised Narendra Modi and even described him as the “bestest leader.” Opposition parties have similarly alleged that some existing Trust figures, including Champat Rai, are politically close to Modi.

But ultimately, Mishra should be judged neither by his praise for Modi nor simply by the fact that he is a decorated former Air Marshal. The real test will be his work over the next five years, whether he can bring greater transparency and accountability to the Trust and help the Ram Temple move beyond the controversies and allegations, including those related to financial irregularities, that have surrounded its administration.

His performance, not his uniform or his political proximity, should decide how this appointment is remembered.

text:
I’m from Kashmir too, and my grandfather often shared beautiful memories of his Kashmiri Pandit friends. He always told me that they were kind-hearted, warm, and friendly people, and that they used to live together like brothers.

He also used to say that, according to his understanding, many Kashmiri Pandits were sent to Jammu by the Government of India during that difficult period, and many of them never returned to Kashmir.

I also have a personal memory connected to this. When I was in Class 7 in 2018, I was taught by a Kashmiri Pandit teacher. He was a very good and kind person, and I still remember those days.

Around 2–3 months before August 2019, he was transferred to Jammu. At that age, I didn’t understand the larger situation around us. I only knew that a teacher I respected was leaving Kashmir.

Years have passed. Today, I’m in my 2nd year of college, but I still remember him and those Class 7 days.

Sometimes, certain people become part of our memories without us even realising how much they will mean to us later.

For me, he is one of those memories—a small part of my childhood that I still remember with respect and warmth. ❤️

This is coming from someone who has been tested deficient for both vitamin D and vitamin B12 on multiple occasions: the information provided in this video about both vitamins is spot on, so thank you for that!

I'd like to add that I recently learned about some digestive health issues I have. Since then, I've also learned that vitamin B12 deficiency can be caused by digestive problems that interfere with the absorption of this vitamin from food, even if you're getting enough of it through your diet.

So, instead of relying on supplements for the rest of your life, consider getting yourself checked out. You might have an underlying health issue that's affecting your body's ability to absorb this vitamin.

One of the teachers at our school reads palms and tells people about their future. At first, most of the students at school did not know about this. However, one day, a boy came to know about it and told a few boys in our class group. After that, some of us asked the teacher about it. At first, however, the teacher was not willing to read our palms. I was not involved in this matter initially, and I was not interested in having my palm read either.

Later, after many requests from the students, the teacher agreed to read the palms of a few boys from our class who already knew about it. Finally, after my friends repeatedly asked me to do it, I also showed my palm to the teacher. After looking at my palm, the teacher said that I had a good future ahead of me and that I would have a bright future.

However, I do not personally believe in predicting the future by reading palms.

Hello Sir, I have a genuine request for you. Please consider launching a proper English-speaking and communication course.

There are many students in India who understand English but struggle when it comes to actually speaking it confidently. They know the grammar, they can understand videos and lectures, but when they have to speak in front of someone, they hesitate, get stuck, or start worrying about making mistakes. I personally feel that English communication is becoming an extremely important skill for students, especially for college, interviews, jobs, presentations, and everyday conversations.

I have explored different apps and courses for improving spoken English, but most of them either focus too much on basic vocabulary and grammar or don't provide a proper structured path from beginner level to confident speaking. I think if you created a course that focuses on practical English, daily conversations, pronunciation, vocabulary, sentence formation, thinking in English, speaking without hesitation, and building confidence, it could be extremely useful for students.

It would be even better if the course included speaking practice, real-life situations, interactive exercises, common mistakes made by Indian students, and a proper day-by-day learning plan. A course that teaches us how to actually USE English rather than just memorize rules would be amazing.

I know you already have a lot of educational content, but I genuinely think an English communication course from you could help a huge number of students who want to improve themselves but don't know where to start.

So Sir, please consider this request. If you ever launch an English-speaking course, I would definitely be interested in joining it. 🙏

text:
Hello Dhruv Sir,
I have another topic request that I believe could lead to a fascinating and genuinely challenging science discussion:
“Extracting Energy from Black Holes — The Physics Behind Penrose Process, Kerr Black Holes, and Rotational Energy.”
The subject is especially intriguing because black holes are usually imagined as objects from which nothing can escape, yet general relativity predicts mechanisms through which energy can, in principle, be extracted from a rotating black hole.

I would be especially interested in a video addressing these questions:

1. If nothing can escape from within the event horizon, how can a rotating black hole nevertheless lose its rotational energy through mechanisms such as the Penrose process or the Blandford–Znajek mechanism? What, precisely, is the physical origin of the extracted energy?

2. The Penrose process relies upon the ergosphere of a Kerr black hole and the existence of negative-energy trajectories relative to an observer at infinity. What does “negative energy” actually mean in curved spacetime, and how does frame dragging make such states physically possible without violating energy conservation?

3. Is there a fundamental upper limit to the amount of energy that can be extracted from a rotating black hole? If so, how is this limit related to the black hole’s dimensionless spin parameter, irreducible mass, horizon area, and the laws of black-hole thermodynamics?

4. Could black-hole energy extraction ever be regarded as a physically realizable energy source rather than merely a theoretical consequence of general relativity? What observational evidence would distinguish genuine rotational-energy extraction from ordinary electromagnetic or accretion-powered processes surrounding active black holes?

I find this topic particularly fascinating because it sits at the intersection of general relativity, quantum theory, astrophysics, and thermodynamics, while challenging the intuitive idea that a black hole can only absorb energy and never give any back.

I would genuinely love to see a detailed video exploring the mathematics and physical intuition behind this.

Thank you for considering the request.

text:
I am from Telangana, but I have always had a deep admiration for Tamil Nadu and its history. I have learned about many great empires, but whenever I study the Chola dynasty, I am amazed by just how advanced and magnificent they were.

Their architecture is simply extraordinary. I have personally visited the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and the temple at Darasuram, and I have spent a lot of time studying their magnificent sculptures and architectural details. You truly have to visit these places in person to understand what I mean—words alone cannot describe their grandeur.

Their achievements were not limited to temples. When you learn about their irrigation works on the Kaveri River, dams, water-management and conservation systems, you cannot help but be amazed at their engineering knowledge and foresight.

The Cholas were great patrons of Shaivism and built magnificent temples dedicated to Lord Shiva. What astonishes me most is that many of these monumental structures have stood for nearly a thousand years and still remain magnificent today.

Thanjavur also has an extraordinary cultural legacy—from the beautiful Tanjore paintings to the Veena and its rich musical traditions.

And there is so much more—the powerful Chola navy, their maritime achievements, overseas expeditions and trade, their well-organised administration, and their remarkable system of village self-governance.

Although I am from Telangana, I have a special love and admiration for Tamil Nadu, its history, culture, architecture and heritage.

I could go on and on—there is simply so much to admire and learn about the Cholas and the incredible legacy they left behind.

नमस्ते ध्रुव जी,
मैं आपसे हाथ जोड़कर एक विनती करना चाहता हूँ।
उत्तर प्रदेश की एक गौशाला में गायों की हालत देखकर दिल रो पड़ता है। इस भीषण गर्मी में कई गायें पानी की एक-एक बूंद के लिए तरस रही हैं। खाने की भी भारी कमी है। जिन बेजुबान जानवरों की सेवा और सुरक्षा की बात की जाती है, वही आज भूख और प्यास से तड़पने को मजबूर हैं।
वे अपनी पीड़ा किसी से कह नहीं सकतीं, शिकायत नहीं कर सकतीं, बस चुपचाप कष्ट सह रही हैं। जब उनकी सूखी आंखें और कमजोर शरीर दिखाई देते हैं, तो मन बहुत दुखी हो जाता है।
आपसे विनम्र निवेदन है कि कृपया इस मुद्दे पर ध्यान दें और यदि संभव हो तो इसकी सच्चाई को सामने लाने के लिए एक वीडियो बनाएं। आपकी आवाज लाखों लोगों तक पहुंचती है। शायद आपकी एक वीडियो इन बेजुबान जीवों की जिंदगी में बदलाव ला सके।
उम्मीद है कि आप इस विनती पर विचार करेंगे।
धन्यवाद।

text:
The history

During the Congress/UPA rule (2004–2014) and throughout prior decades before recent legal changes, the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and Election Commissioners (ECs) were appointed through a process governed directly by executive discretion under Article 324(2) of the Indian Constitution.

Appointment Process Under Congress/UPA Era

1. Executive Nomination:
There was no statutory selection committee, formal search panel, or parliamentary law specifying how candidates were chosen.
The Union Cabinet/Council of Ministers, led by the Prime Minister, directly selected the name from senior Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officers (typically the top-ranking civil servants or retiring officers).

2. Presidential Appointment:
Under Article 324(2), the President of India formally appointed the CEC based on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers.

3. Convention of Elevation:
A well-established convention was followed where the senior-most Election Commissioner was elevated to the post of Chief Election Commissioner upon the vacancy of the top office.

Key Milestones & Comparisons

Convention Before 2023: For decades (under Congress as well as subsequent non-Congress governments until 2023), the executive possessed sole authority to select candidates without requiring consultation with the judiciary or Opposition leaders.

Supreme Court Interim Ruling (March 2023): In Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court mandated that appointments be made on the recommendation of a 3-member committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition, and the Chief Justice of India (CJI) to preserve independence.

Current Law (2023 Onward): Parliament passed the Chief Election

Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, which replaced the CJI on the selection panel with a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister, alongside the PM and the Leader of the Opposition.

So who did it democratically in consultation

text: My mom died due to Leukemia when I was 2. I stayed with my maternal grandparents since I was born because my father was in Military. When I was 5, my dad forcefully took me away from my grandparents to live with him. I didn't even know he was my father, I just heard about him. I was a very talkative kid when I am around my grandparents, but with him, I couldn't look upto his eyes. He would forcefully fed me pork once, I said, I don't like pork and it makes me puke, he said I was being selective and fed me nonetheless, I puke at the dinner on the plate itself. He beat the shit out of me. He also said, I should go to toilet while eating. One time, when visiting his friends home while eating dinner, I wet myself peeing while eating because of fear of asking to go to toilet. I was beaten for every other small mistakes till high school. I can't start a conversion with him, couldn't look him in the eyes. My self esteem was very low in life. After high school, I wanted to join Military, he forced me to go to engineering.I had  No choice but to agree. I got fed up after 2 semesters, I didn't like engineering and hated it. I didn't know I was so depressed for more than 6 years. When 2nd semester finished and while at home during vacation, I said I can't do engineering anymore, then we went to argue. Since then I had always sense of revolt inside me, I didn't know what happened to me. I search online and came to know i was suffering from depression. I got into argument with stepmother as well. In 2024, I left thier house and came back to my maternal grandparents home where I felt loved, free of pressure and confidence. I'm a farmer now, helping my grandparents and villagers with the knowledge I have. I serve as head of the village. Honesty I don't remember a single good thing between me and my father. All I remember is bad memories and sometimes I feel so angry looking back at it. I hope He and Stepmom are doing good. Words cannot describe what I have gobe through in life. This video should be watched by every parents even In Bhutan. Our Bhutanese parents are like Indian parents only. But I promise I will never be like my father when I became a father.

text:
याद आ गया? बहुत बढ़िया! जैसलमेर के पास स्थित कुलधरा गाँव की कहानी वाकई बेहद दिलचस्प और रहस्यमयी है।
अगर सीधे शब्दों में कहें, तो वैज्ञानिक या ऐतिहासिक रूप से वहाँ किसी भूत-प्रेत या साये का कोई सबूत नहीं है। लेकिन, इस गाँव के रातों-रात खाली होने की कहानी और यहाँ का सन्नाटा इसे "भूतिया" का टैग ज़रूर दिला देता है।
मामला असल में क्या है, इसे थोड़ा समझ लेते हैं:
1. लोककथा (कहानी क्या है?)
कहा जाता है कि करीब 200 साल पहले यह पालीवाल ब्राह्मणों का एक समृद्ध गाँव हुआ करता था। जैसलमेर के दीवान सालिम सिंह की नज़र गाँव के प्रधान की बेटी पर पड़ गई और वह जबरन उससे शादी करना चाहता था। अपनी बेटियों के सम्मान की रक्षा के लिए कुलधरा और आसपास के 84 गाँवों के लोग एक ही रात में गाँव खाली करके चले गए। जाते-जाते वे श्राप दे गए कि यहाँ दोबारा कोई कभी नहीं बस पाएगा।
2. इतिहास और विज्ञान क्या कहते हैं?
इतिहासकारों और रिसर्च के मुताबिक, लोगों के पलायन की वजह कोई भूत या श्राप नहीं, बल्कि कुछ और थी:
पानी की भारी कमी: रेगिस्तान में पानी के स्रोत और कुएँ सूख चुके थे, जिससे वहाँ रहना नामुमकिन हो गया था।
भूकंप और प्राकृतिक आपदा: कुछ शोध (जैसे 2017 का पैलियोसीस्मिक सर्वे) बताते हैं कि उस दौर में आए बड़े भूकंप के कारण घरों को भारी नुकसान हुआ था, जिसकी वजह से लोगों को पलायन करना पड़ा।
भारी टैक्स: दीवान सालिम सिंह द्वारा वसूला जाने वाला बेहिसाब टैक्स भी एक बड़ी वजह था।
3. फिर भूत की बातें क्यों होती हैं?
यह अब एक मशहूर टूरिस्ट स्पॉट है। खंडहरों का अकेलापन, सुनसान माहौल और हवाओं की आवाज़ मिलकर एक अजीब सा डर पैदा करती हैं, जिसे लोग अक्सर भूतिया मान लेते हैं। कुछ पैरानॉर्मल इन्वेस्टिगेटर्स ने वहाँ अजीब गतिविधियाँ महसूस करने का दावा ज़रूर किया, लेकिन विज्ञान इसकी पुष्टि नहीं करता।
निष्कर्ष: कुलधरा में कोई भूत नहीं है, वह बस एक ऐतिहासिक और खूबसूरत 'घोस्ट टाउन' (उजड़ा हुआ गाँव) है, जो अपनी रहस्यमयी कहानी के लिए जाना जाता है।

text:
पहले की सरकारों में नैतिक जिम्मेदारी लेते हुए मंत्री इस्तीफा दे दिया करते थे, लेकिन आज जवाबदेही का वह स्तर दिखाई नहीं देता। शायद अभी आपको यह बात समझ न आए, लेकिन जब आपके बच्चे बड़े होकर प्रतियोगी परीक्षाओं की तैयारी करेंगे, दिन-रात मेहनत करेंगे और फिर पेपर लीक जैसे मामलों के कारण उनका हक किसी ऐसे व्यक्ति को मिल जाएगा, जिसने लाखों रुपये देकर सीट हासिल की हो, तब आपको एहसास होगा कि इस्तीफे की मांग क्यों उठती है।

मैं किसी राजनीतिक पार्टी के पक्ष या विपक्ष में नहीं हूँ। मैं केवल जवाबदेही और निष्पक्ष व्यवस्था की बात कर रहा हूँ। आज कुछ मंत्रियों और नेताओं पर ऐसे सवाल उठ रहे हैं, जिनका जवाब जनता को मिलना चाहिए। लोकतंत्र में सत्ता जनता की सेवा के लिए होती है, न कि अपने परिवार और करीबियों को आगे बढ़ाने के लिए। अगर किसी पर आरोप लगते हैं, तो निष्पक्ष जाँच होनी चाहिए और दोष सिद्ध होने पर उचित कार्रवाई भी।

सवाल यह नहीं है कि सरकार किस पार्टी की है, सवाल यह है कि क्या सत्ता में बैठे लोगों की कोई नैतिक जिम्मेदारी भी है? जनता से यह उम्मीद नहीं की जा सकती कि वह हर सवाल पर आँखें बंद कर ले। लोकतंत्र में अंधसमर्थन नहीं, जवाबदेही जरूरी है।

दोस्तों, मैं Bhangarh Fort का लोकल रहने वाला हूँ, और जो सच है वो शेयर करना चाहता हूँ।

सबसे पहले—यहाँ “भूत-प्रेत” वाली बात ज़्यादातर कहानियों और इंटरनेट की वजह से फैली है। मैं खुद कई बार रात में किले के अंदर जा चुका हूँ, और हमारे गाँव के लोग भी जाते रहते हैं। आज तक ना मैंने और ना ही किसी जानने वाले ने यहाँ कुछ “अलौकिक” देखा या महसूस किया।

हाँ, रात में अजीब आवाज़ें जरूर आती हैं—लेकिन उसका कारण बिल्कुल साफ है। यह किला पहाड़ों और जंगल के बीच है, और पास में Sariska Tiger Reserve का इलाका आता है। यहाँ जंगली जानवरों की आवाज़ें, हवा, और खाली खंडहर—ये सब मिलकर माहौल को डरावना बना देते हैं।

ASI (पुरातत्व विभाग) ने भी जो रात में रुकने का नियम बनाया है, वो “भूतों” की वजह से नहीं बल्कि सेफ्टी के लिए है—क्योंकि यह पूरा जंगल एरिया है।

To the Nobel Voice, Dhruv Rathee,

I am writing to make a humble request — to give your voice for the people of the nation of Cuba.

The citizens of Cuba are living in darkness. There is no proper electricity, no fuel for transportation, and no sufficient clean water to drink. The people are struggling every single day just to survive the most basic needs of life. Prices have more than tripled since 2021, and thousands of families are living without proper food. The most affected are the elderly, the sick, and the children.

I, and many other people, can understand this pain and raise our voices at our own level. But you, Dhruv brother, are different from us. When you speak, people listen. You can make millions of voices unite and start a movement of change — and the people of Cuba desperately need that awareness to reach the world right now.

People from India, from different nations and different corners of the world, can come together because of your one video. Many people who are unaware today can become aware tomorrow, and that awareness itself can become a movement of change.

I just want the people of Cuba to be known. I believe deeply that even awareness and communication can start a huge change.

I do not know exactly how this will happen — but I know in my heart that it has to happen.

I and many people will be truly grateful for your support, Dhruv. Even a small mention, a video, or a conversation can give hope to millions who are suffering in silence.

Thank you so much for your time. I wish more success, happiness, and good health to you and your family.

Thank you,
Sahil Reshma

text:
Saudi Arabia is a useful example of how financial strength and access to sophisticated military technology do not automatically translate into battlefield effectiveness. The Kingdom has invested heavily in modern aircraft, air-defence systems, armoured platforms, and other advanced equipment, much of it comparable to what is operated by major military powers. However, historically, Saudi forces have had considerably less exposure to prolonged, high-intensity conventional warfare and large-scale combat operations.

From a military-historical perspective, the distinction is important: possessing advanced equipment is one thing; developing the doctrine, command experience, tactical proficiency, logistics, and institutional knowledge required to employ it effectively under combat conditions is another. This is not necessarily an economic question, but economics can influence defence capability by determining what equipment a state can acquire, maintain, and sustain. Ultimately, technology provides capability, while experience and military institutions determine how effectively that capability is converted into combat power.

text:
I think you should make a detailed video on this topic. My concern is that India still does not have enough globally competitive, India-owned technology ecosystems that we can fully depend on. We use foreign operating systems, smartphone platforms, cloud infrastructure, software, communication platforms, and many other critical technologies.
Just imagine a hypothetical situation: what would happen if the US government asked American companies to completely stop operating in India and withdraw their services and technology from the country? How much of our banking, healthcare, government infrastructure, businesses, communications, and other critical sectors would actually continue functioning?
This is the question I think deserves serious research. It is not only about GPS or smartphones. It is about technological sovereignty and strategic dependency—who owns the platforms, infrastructure, operating systems, cloud services, software, standards, and technologies that our economy depends on.
India has been independent for nearly 80 years, but where are the Indian technologies and platforms that have become truly global at the same scale? Where is our globally dominant operating system, cloud platform, social-media platform, communication platform, or programming ecosystem? We have enormous engineering and scientific talent, but why haven't we produced more globally dominant technology companies and foundational technologies ourselves?
Even programming languages and major software ecosystems that we use every day largely originated outside India. For example, JavaScript originated at Netscape, while Python was originally created in the Netherlands. �
MDN Web Docs +1
India does have indigenous technology efforts—such as NavIC, our own regional satellite-navigation system, and BOSS Linux, an Indian GNU/Linux distribution developed by C-DAC. � But my question is: why haven't these kinds of technologies reached much larger global adoption and strategic importance?
ISRO +1
And what about companies like TCS, Wipro and Infosys? Why are we still primarily known for providing IT services rather than creating and owning more of the world's foundational technology platforms?
I think this deserves a serious, data-driven video—not just a discussion about GDP or economic growth, but about technological independence, infrastructure ownership, strategic dependencies, and what could happen to India in a worst-case scenario. Please research this deeply and make a video on it. 🇮🇳

text:
The same long-working-hour culture exists in India as well, particularly in certain industries and manufacturing environments. Large manufacturing companies in India also operate 24×7 through rotating shifts where continuous production is required.

However, there are important differences when comparing India and China. China has historically had a much more established factory-dormitory model, where workers can live close to or within accommodation provided near the workplace. India also has worker hostels and factory-provided accommodation in some manufacturing sectors, but many workers still commute to factories, sometimes spending 2–3 hours a day travelling by company shuttle or public transport.

Therefore, comparing only the number of working hours does not give the complete picture. Commute time, accommodation, shift patterns, working conditions, productivity expectations, and—most importantly—salary and overall compensation all need to be considered.

Also, we should be careful about comparing manufacturing workers with employees in BPOs, KPOs or other service-sector companies. Manufacturing operations often involve production lines, machinery utilisation and continuous shift-based operations, so the nature of work and the economics of working hours are fundamentally different.

1. "Code of conduct" argument

Yes, the Jharkhand protest has a good code of conduct, and I respect that. But just because another protest followed a different style doesn't mean it was wrong. Different protests use different methods depending on the situation.

2. "Nobody was talking about this protest."

Really?

The protest started on 29 July, and within a week it got media attention. You yourself are making a video on it, and mainstream media has already covered it. So please stop pretending nobody cared. You're making assumptions, not arguments.

3. "They are serving food to the police."

You praise the Jharkhand students for serving food to the police and respecting them. That's great.

But for your information, the same thing happened at Jantar Mantar. Students there also served food, gave water, and even used fans to help police personnel after being beaten by the police and RAF. How would you know that? Were you there? Or are you just assuming what happened because it fits your narrative?

4. "They chant Vande Mataram."

Again... as if this never happened at Jantar Mantar.

Students there also raised patriotic slogans. But you conveniently ignored that because it doesn't fit the comparison you're trying to create.

5. "Jharkhand has no single leader unlike CJP."

That's misleading.

Even in the CJP protest there were multiple student groups working together. The spokesperson was just the public face, just like the person leading the hunger strike is the public face here.

Also, you mentioned that person is an RSS worker. Fine. I am not saying that makes this protest wrong. I'm simply saying political backgrounds don't suddenly become irrelevant only when they suit your narrative.

6. Closed-door meetings

Your soft manipulation here was amazing.

When CJP leaders met behind closed doors, you implied something suspicious. But when the Jharkhand students demand open meetings in front of cameras, suddenly you present it as the ideal approach.

Apply the same standard to everyone instead of changing it depending on the protest.

7. Delhi gets more attention

Let's be honest.

Any protest in Delhi naturally gets more eyeballs because it's the capital of India. That doesn't make protests in other states less important.

I'm not saying only Delhi protests matter. I'm saying this is the reality of media coverage. Stop pretending this obvious fact proves something else.

Finally, thank you for covering the Jharkhand protest. At least you addressed it.

And thank God this protest is happening under a non-BJP state government. Otherwise, maybe we would've gotten another video focusing more on everything except the actual issue, just like what happened with the CJP protest.

I genuinely hope you reflect on your own biases and start asking the same tough questions to every government instead of changing your standards depending on the situation.

And one last thing for Niyu.

The ending of the video suggests that discussing problems or demanding accountability isn't as important as talking about solutions.

I completely disagree.

Discussion and accountability are the first step toward solving any problem. If people don't raise issues publicly, no one is forced to fix them.

The CJP protest itself proved that public discussion matters. Solutions don't appear out of nowhere they begin with people questioning the system.

text: I have been thinking recently that the government should implement a mandatory retirement age of 55 to 60 across all professions, from street vendors and auto drivers to top government ministers. text:
As the owner of a 2017 Bajaj Avenger 220 Street, I've noticed a significant decline in its performance over the years.
When it was new, the bike delivered smooth power, strong acceleration, and a real-world fuel economy of around 30–35 km/l. From 2017 to 2025, the engine was never opened, yet it remained highly reliable. I regularly rode long distances, including Delhi–Rohtak, Rohtak–Gurgaon, Sonipat, Panipat, and Gohana, without any major issues.
However, after 2025, the bike's behavior changed noticeably:
Fuel economy dropped to around 20–22 km/l.
The engine now demands earlier gear shifts.
Power and pickup have reduced significantly.
The bike starts overheating after just 10–12 km of riding.
Sometimes it suddenly stalls as if the fuel tank is empty, even when there is sufficient petrol.
On those occasions, the engine won't start unless I use the choke.
I have maintained this motorcycle with great care, which makes these changes disappointing.

Viewers, recognizing this, have begun shifting towards YouTubers, valuing the ability to choose their content—even with its imperfections.

Now, after the Samay Raina controversy, it's clear—TV media will do anything to crush YouTubers. But they won’t win! YouTubers are smarter, more united, and unstoppable. If they rise together, TV media is finished!

text:
ऐतिहासिक पृष्ठभूमियह
किला सरिस्का राष्ट्रीय उद्यान के पास अरावली पहाड़ियों के बीच बसा है।एक समय में यह किला नहीं, बल्कि हजारों घरों और बाजारों वाला एक समृद्ध और आबाद शहर था।सन् 1783 के आसपास भयंकर अकाल और आपदा के कारण यहाँ के लोग शहर छोड़कर चले गए, जिससे यह वीरान हो गया।राजकुमारी रत्नावती और तांत्रिक की कहानी
लोक कथाओं के अनुसार, भानगढ़ की सुंदर राजकुमारी रत्नावती पर सिंधिया सेवा नाम का एक तांत्रिक मोहित हो गया था।तांत्रिक ने राजकुमारी को वश में करने के लिए काले जादू वाले इत्र की शिसी भेजी।राजकुमारी को साजिश का पता चला तो उसने इत्र की शीशी को एक चट्टान पर फेंक दिया, जिससे पत्थर तांत्रिक पर आ गिरा और उसकी मौत हो गई।मरने से पहले तांत्रिक ने श्राप दिया कि पूरा नगर नष्ट हो जाएगा और यहाँ कभी किसी की शांतिपूर्ण आत्मा नहीं बसेगी।बाबा बालकनाथ का श्रापएक अन्य प्रचलित कथा के अनुसार, राजा ने जब किले का निर्माण कराया था, तब वहाँ एक तपस्वी बाबा बालकनाथ रहते थे।शर्त यह थी कि किले की परछाई बाबा की कुटिया पर नहीं पड़नी चाहिए।राजा के वंशजों ने जब किले को बहुत ऊँचा कर दिया, तब उसकी छाया बाबा की तपस्थली पर पड़ी, जिसके श्राप से यह नगर खंडहर बन गया।रात के वक्त पाबंदी का कारणभारतीय पुरातत्व सर्वेक्षण (ASI) के नियमों के अनुसार अंधेरा होने के बाद यहाँ रुकना मना है।लोगों का मानना है कि रात में यहाँ अजीब आवाजें आती हैं, लेकिन वैज्ञानिक और प्रशासनिक तौर पर सुरक्षा व वन्यजीवों का खतरा ही इसका मुख्य कारण है।भानगढ़ के किले के खंडहरों और वहाँ की बनावट को समझने के लिए इस वीडियो को देखें

text:
There was a real Pharaoh named Rudamun in ancient history, but he is not historically linked to Prophet Yusuf.
Dynasty: He was the final pharaoh of the 23rd Dynasty (around 750 BCE).
The Timeline Gap: Most scholars place the life of Prophet Yusuf much earlier—either during the Hyksos period (around 1600 BCE) or the Middle Kingdom (around 1800–1900 BCE).
The Difference: The historical Rudamun lived nearly 1,000 years after the era typically associated with Prophet Yusuf. The show likely used the name to give the character an authentic Egyptian feel.

text:
Captain I understood. It's a clean case of clear wind sheer and turbulence.

I am also a part of the aviation industry working on the commercial side. The last trip was in February from Doha to Trivandrum with my family. Total 5 pax including two adults and two kids (4 and 9 years) and one infant (4 months). We were flyingbon Qatar Airways (QR506) A320 flight and we encountered severe turbulence three times. We're in the 1at row of the economy cabin. We encountered this incident hardly one and half hours before landing. My elder daughter was a Young Solo Traveler for two years as she was studying in India and she used to travel twice in a year on Qatar Airways as Young Solo Traveler. Once she told me she experienced a slight difficulty of turbulence (she don't even know the word turbulence). She just explained with hand signals. Flight flew like this. I thought she was bluffing. After a few months I experienced the same while I went to India for a funeral. So I understood she was not bluffing. But last time it was hectic. When the first turbulence started I looked at the watch it was almost the same time as what I experienced during my last trip. My wife got a little bit afraid and I took the baby and held him with me and I told her to fasten her seatbelt and kids. After 5 or 10 mins we encountered severe turbulence and it lasted for 5mins. After 20 to 30mins we had massive turbulence and the aircraft was going up and down. I always play live maps on the screen so I noticed the altitude changes as well. It lasted almost ten minutes and l heard many passengers crying. Most of them were sleeping and suddenly woke up because of turbulence. I never had such an incident in my life. But during the third turbulence i felt like suddenly engines are shutting down or going to idle. Because I was sitting in the 8th row where the wings were connected. So the engine sound is clearly audible. I still don't understand why I felt that there are changes happening in the engines rotation

text:
A few observations regarding the Jorhat AN-32 accident:

First, the runway itself was not the problem. Jorhat has a well-maintained runway of over 10,000 feet, recently re-carpeted, equipped with CAT-II ILS, and maintained to ICAO standards. It is a major transport airbase that has supported transport operations for decades and now also handles fighter operations. The runway infrastructure, markings and operational facilities are of a high standard.

From the available footage, the aircraft appears to have touched down and continued its landing roll normally for approximately 50- 100 metres before veering left. What exactly caused the aircraft to leave the runway can only be determined through the Court of Inquiry, analysis of the Flight Data Recorder (FDR), Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR), technical evidence and crew statements. Any discussion before that remains speculation.

However, once the aircraft crossed the runway shoulder, another major factor came into play. The aircraft entered an open monsoon drainage ditch located alongside the runway environment. The sudden impact with this drain appears to have significantly aggravated the accident sequence. Had this drain been covered, protected or otherwise mitigated, the aircraft might have continued rolling and the severity of the accident could potentially have been reduced. Such ground hazards deserve serious scrutiny.

The emergency response visible in the videos is also concerning. One pilot can be seen exiting the aircraft while immediate rescue assistance is not yet visible. Personnel already present near the accident site, including bird-control staff and grass-cutting personnel, were among the closest individuals to the aircraft and could potentially have provided immediate assistance during those critical first moments.

Most concerning is the apparent delay in Crash Fire Tender (CFT) response. In aviation emergencies, seconds matter. Response and control times exist for a reason, and a delay of even 10–20 seconds can make a significant difference to survivability. Based on the available footage, the response does not appear to meet the level of urgency expected at a major operational airbase.

Overall, this appears to be a classic chain-of-events accident rather than a single-point failure. If there was a technical malfunction, that was one link in the chain. The open monsoon drain was another. The apparent shortcomings in emergency response may have been another. Aviation accidents are rarely caused by one factor alone; they are usually the result of multiple failures aligning at the same time.

It was a very unfortunate incident, and the final conclusions must come from the official investigation. But from an aviation perspective, this accident appears to highlight the importance of not only aircraft serviceability, but also airfield safety infrastructure, hazard management and rapid emergency response.

text:
This is not the first occurrence of this type. The aircraft may have experienced a propeller withdrawal malfunction, which the pilot normally initiates shortly after touchdown before applying the brakes, when the blade pitch reduces to approximately 2° as part of the fixed-RPM propeller system operation. Even at minimum power, the blade pitch remains around 15°, which can still produce sufficient forward thrust. This aircraft is also not equipped with thrust reversal.

The issue may have been related to the propeller withdrawal system, as only one propeller appears to have withdrawn. The tiller provides directional control only during taxi operations, whereas during take-off and landing modes, the aircraft relies on rudder pedal input for approximately 10° of directional control on either side.

Asymmetric braking is another possible factor; however, it appears less likely because the propeller withdrawal seems to have occurred before the application of braking.

Goan culture is also best experienced through its food. There are many authentic Goan restaurants where you can discover traditional home-style dishes, fresh seafood, local breads and recipes passed down through generations. You could visit Chef Fernando’s Nostalgia in Raia, Martin’s Corner in Betalbatim, The Fisherman’s Wharf in Cavelossim and Palácio do Deão in Quepem for a unique heritage dining experience.

text:
I have X200T, and I have noticed that in portrait mode there's too much AI processing irrespective of lighting conditions. For example, it took a photo in which the subject's smile was slightly distorted, specifically it overdid the lips, and it darkened the lines between the teeth. I like the overall result, but when you zoom in, you can find the AI's work.

I know smartphone cameras have physical limitations, so they have to rely on processing, but I don't like how it touches facial features. I don't find such facial distortions in other brands.

I hope you make a specific video regarding AI processing in portrait mode, especially how it affects facial features like lips, teeth, eyes, skin texture and the overall expression — not the AI zooming capabilities.

I would also request you to raise this issue with Vivo and urge them to stop or at least reduce this kind of aggressive processing on facial features. There should also be an option for users to completely turn off Beauty Mode, so that it doesn't apply any beauty processing and doesn't even show any beauty effect in the viewfinder. Setting the beauty level to zero shouldn't mean that some processing is still happening in the background.

I really like the overall camera output of the X200T, but I would prefer a more natural portrait processing option where the person's actual facial features are preserved instead of being modified by AI.
